summary: This experimental RFC describes boundary-node behavior for the Controlled Load mode of Pre-Congestion Notification, a measurement-based load control approach using three marking states: not-marked, threshold-marked and excess-traffic-marked.

plainLanguage.summary:
Pre-Congestion Notification, or PCN, lets a network react before it congests. Edge nodes label packets when traffic passes a configured limit, and a control point uses those labels to decide whether to admit new flows or to shut some existing ones down.

This RFC describes one way to run PCN, called Controlled Load. It uses three marking states and is meant for networks that carry voice and video.

questions: what is pcn controlled load mode
how do pcn boundary nodes behave in cl mode
what is the congestion level estimate in pcn
how does pcn decide to terminate flows
what is the cle-limit in pcn
how does pcn cl mode mark traffic
subtitle: How edge nodes use three marking states to admit new flows and terminate existing ones before a network congests.

tldr.problem: A network carrying inelastic traffic such as voice and video must protect the quality of the flows it has already admitted, and it needs to react before congestion actually happens.
tldr.mechanism: Every link meters the traffic and marks PCN packets when a configured rate is exceeded. An egress node reports the marked rates to a decision point, which either admits or blocks new flows and can terminate existing ones.
tldr.outcome: This RFC defines the Controlled Load (CL) mode of PCN, one of a series of experimental boundary-node behaviors. It uses three marking states and expects admission control of micro-flows at the edge of the network.

today: RFC 6661 is an Experimental document, published for examination, experimental implementation and evaluation, and it has not been obsoleted. The RFC calls itself one of a series of possible PCN boundary-node behaviors; the sibling document RFC 6662 specifies the Single Marking mode.

sections.title: What Pre-Congestion Notification Does
sections.content:
Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) protects the quality of service of inelastic traffic inside a Diffserv domain. Inelastic traffic is traffic such as voice and video that cannot slow down when the network is busy. The overall architecture is described in RFC 5559.

PCN uses two mechanisms. Admission control decides whether to admit or block a new flow request. Flow termination decides, in abnormal circumstances, whether to terminate some of the existing flows. Both work from measurements taken on every link of the PCN-domain: the overall rate of PCN traffic is metered, and PCN packets are marked when certain configured rates are exceeded. Those configured rates are below the rate of the link, so the boundary nodes learn about a possible overload before any congestion occurs.

This RFC specifies the Controlled Load (CL) mode of the PCN boundary-node behavior. It uses three PCN marking states: not-marked, threshold-marked and excess-traffic-marked. The companion document RFC 6662 specifies the Single Marking (SM) mode, which uses two states. The RFC notes that the words block and terminate describe several possible courses of action, and that the choice between them is a matter of local policy.
sections.plainLanguage: PCN gives a network a way to act before it congests. Edge nodes mark packets when traffic passes a configured limit, and a control point uses the marks to decide whether to let new flows in or to shut some existing ones down.

sections.title: The Terms the RFC Defines
sections.content:
The RFC borrows most of its vocabulary from RFC 5559 and RFC 6660 and adds a few terms of its own. A Decision Point is the node that decides which flows to admit and which to terminate. It can be the PCN-ingress-node itself or a separate centralized control node, and in either case the PCN-ingress-node is the point where the decisions are enforced.

Three rates are measured for each ingress-egress-aggregate, that is, for each group of flows that shares an ingress node and an egress node. The NM-rate is the octets per second of PCN traffic in not-marked packets, the ThM-rate counts threshold-marked traffic and the ETM-rate counts excess-traffic-marked traffic. The PCN-sent-rate is the rate at which an ingress node is receiving PCN traffic destined for a given aggregate.

The congestion level estimate (CLE) is the ratio of PCN-marked to total PCN traffic, measured in octets, received for an aggregate during one measurement period. It is used to derive the PCN-admission-state, which is either admit or block, and it is also used by the report suppression procedure. The sustainable aggregate rate (SAR) is the estimated maximum rate of PCN traffic that an aggregate can carry at a given moment without risking a degradation of quality of service for the admitted flows.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC names the node that makes the decisions the Decision Point. It also names three measured traffic rates, one for each marking state, and one number that compares marked traffic with all traffic.

sections.title: Collecting and Reporting Traffic Rates
sections.content:
At the end of every measurement period, the PCN-egress-node meters the PCN traffic it received and calculates the NM-rate, the ThM-rate and the ETM-rate for each ingress-egress-aggregate passing through it. The length of a measurement period is the configurable value T_meas. Unless report suppression is switched on, the node must report the latest values of those three rates to the Decision Point each time it calculates them.

As a configurable option, the egress node may also record the identifiers of the PCN flows for which excess-traffic-marked packets were observed during the interval, and it must then include them in the report. If the set is large, for example more than 20 flows, the node may record only the most recently marked flows. The Decision Point can start with those flows when it selects flows for termination, which helps in networks that route one aggregate over several paths and where only some paths are congested.

Report suppression is a configurable option that reduces signalling traffic. With it, the node calculates the CLE for each measurement interval and sends a report only when the latest CLE is greater than the CLE-reporting-threshold, or when the previous interval's CLE was greater than it. It must also send a report once T_maxsuppress has passed since the last one, whatever the CLE says. The result is at least one report per interval of T_maxsuppress + T_meas, which tells the Decision Point that the node and the communication path are still working.
sections.plainLanguage: The egress node measures traffic over short periods and reports how much of it carried each mark. It may skip reports when nothing much is happening, but it has to report at least once every few seconds so the Decision Point knows it is still there.

sections.title: Admitting and Terminating Flows
sections.content:
The Decision Point determines the PCN-admission-state for an aggregate each time it receives a report. It compares the CLE, which it should take from the report or else calculate itself, with a configurable CLE-limit. If the CLE is less than the limit the state is admit, otherwise it is block. When the state is admit the Decision Point should allow new flows to be admitted to the aggregate; when it is block it should not.

Termination starts when a report includes a non-zero ETM-rate for an aggregate. The Decision Point then requests the PCN-sent-rate from the ingress node and waits for both that answer and the next report from the egress node. If the next report also shows a non-zero ETM-rate, the Decision Point estimates the sustainable aggregate rate as SAR = NM-rate + ThM-rate and works out the amount of traffic to terminate as PCN-sent-rate - SAR. If that difference is positive it selects flows to terminate, using upper rate limits for the individual flows so that it does not remove too much, and it should first consider the flows the egress node reported as excess-traffic-marked.

When a report does not arrive, the Decision Point uses a timer called t_recvFail. The timeout T_fail is the configurable duration T_crit when report suppression is not deployed, and also when the last report carried a CLE greater than the reporting threshold. Otherwise it is 3 * T_maxsuppress. When the timer expires the Decision Point should notify management, and local policy may then block new flows destined for that egress node until a report arrives. If a request for the PCN-sent-rate goes unanswered, the request is repeated once, and the ETM-rate is used as an estimate of how much traffic to terminate.
sections.plainLanguage: The control point compares the share of traffic that carries a mark against a limit. Below the limit it lets new flows in; above the limit it blocks them and can shut existing flows down to bring the rate back down.

sections.title: Timers and Recommended Values
sections.content:
Four timers drive the procedures. t_meas runs at the egress node, one per ingress-egress-aggregate, and expires when it reaches T_meas; the node then calculates the three rates and reports them. t_maxsuppress also runs at the egress node and expires at T_maxsuppress, after which a report is sent whatever the CLE says. t_recvFail runs at the Decision Point and expires at T_fail. t_sndFail is used only by a centralized Decision Point, one per outstanding request for the PCN-sent-rate, and expires at T_crit.

The recommended values are all tied to an intended PCN reaction time of 1 to 3 seconds, and the RFC says they rest on judgement rather than on operational experience or mathematical derivation. The value of T_meas is recommended to be on the order of 100 to 500 ms, which trades the demands on the egress node, the Decision Point and the network against how quickly PCN reacts. The value of T_maxsuppress is recommended to be on the order of 3 to 6 seconds, for similar reasons. T_crit should not be less than 3 * T_meas, because a smaller value would cause too many management notifications after transient trouble, and a reasonable upper bound for it is on the order of 3 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC suggests measuring traffic every 100 to 500 milliseconds and checking in with the control point every 3 to 6 seconds. It aims to react to overload within one to three seconds.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to RFC 5559 for the general security considerations for PCN and adds one point of its own. A centralized Decision Point is itself a trusted entity. Using one means there is an interface on the PCN-ingress-node through which policy decisions are communicated, and that interface is a point of vulnerability that must be protected from denial-of-service attacks.

The deployment section adds that the information needed for a centralized Decision Point and each PCN edge node to authenticate one another has to be prepared for them. The per-domain behavior section also notes that reusing the ECN bits for PCN marking could interfere with the use of end-to-end ECN, and points to RFC 6660 for the actions that can be taken to protect ECN signalling.
sections.plainLanguage: A centralized control point is trusted, so the link that carries its decisions into the network is a weak point that must not be easy to flood. The nodes also need information that lets them check each other's identity.

items.title: Not-marked (NM)
items.text: PCN packets carrying the not-marked codepoint. Their rate is counted as NM-rate.

items.title: Threshold-marked (ThM)
items.text: PCN packets marked by the threshold-meter, whose reference rate on a link is the PCN-admissible-rate.

items.title: Excess-traffic-marked (ETM)
items.text: PCN packets marked by the excess-traffic-meter, whose reference rate on a link is the PCN-supportable-rate.
